title: Yesterday I went to Conamara
goal: Talk about what happened using the past tense, and make it negative or a question.
bekal: form the past tense: *d'ól mé*, *cheannaigh mé*, *d'fhan mé*
use *níor* and *ar*, which both bring séimhiú
recognize the eleven irregular past forms

dialogs.title: Comhrá — An deireadh seachtaine a bhí ann
dialogs.intro: Monday morning in class. Aoife asks Budi how his weekend was.

lines.speaker: Aoife:
lines.text: Dia duit, a Bhudi. Conas a bhí an deireadh seachtaine?
lines.id: Hi, Budi. How was your weekend?
lines.literal: God to-you, O Budi. how that was the end week-of?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Bhí sé ar fheabhas! Chuaigh mé go Conamara Dé Sathairn.
lines.id: Amazing! I went to Conamara on Saturday.
lines.literal: was it on excellence! went I to Conamara day Saturday.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Thaitin go mór. Chonaic mé an fharraige agus na sléibhte.
lines.id: Very much. I saw the sea and the mountains.
lines.literal: pleased greatly. saw I the sea and the mountains.

lines.speaker: Aoife:
lines.text: An raibh an aimsir go maith?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ní raibh! Bhí sé ag cur báistí ar maidin. Ach ghlan sé tráthnóna.
lines.id: No! It rained in the morning. But it cleared up in the afternoon.
lines.literal: wasn't! was it at putting rain-of in the morning. but cleared it afternoon.

lines.speaker: Aoife:
lines.id: And what did you do then?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: D'ith mé dinnéar i mbialann bheag agus d'ól mé tae.
lines.id: I had dinner in a little restaurant and drank tea.
lines.literal: ate I dinner in restaurant small and drank I tea.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Labhair! Bhí gach duine ag labhairt Gaeilge ansin.
lines.id: I did! Everyone there was speaking Irish.
lines.literal: spoke! was every person at speaking Irish there.

lines.speaker: Aoife:
lines.text: Sin an Ghaeltacht duit. Ar cheannaigh tú aon rud?
lines.id: That's the Gaeltacht for you. Did you buy anything?
lines.literal: that the Gaeltacht to-you. question-past bought you any thing?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Cheannaigh mé leabhar. Níor fhan mé i bhfad, ach bhí lá iontach agam.
lines.id: I bought a book. I didn't stay long, but it was a wonderful day.
lines.literal: bought I book. not-past stayed I in length, but was day wonderful at-me.

notes: **The past tense changes the first letter, not the ending.** Verbs starting with a **consonant** get séimhiú: *ceannaigh* → *cheannaigh mé*, *glan* → *ghlan mé*, *tuig* → *thuig mé*. Verbs starting with a **vowel or f** get *d'* in front: *ól* → *d'ól mé*, *ith* → *d'ith mé*, *fan* → *d'fhan mé*, *éirigh* → *d'éirigh mé*. There are no endings to learn for different persons — *cheannaigh mé*, *cheannaigh tú*, *cheannaigh sé* are all the same.

**Níor and ar both bring séimhiú.** Unlike the present, where *ní* brings séimhiú but *an* brings urú, in the past **both** bring séimhiú: *níor cheannaigh mé*, *ar cheannaigh tú?* Note too that *d'* disappears once *níor* or *ar* comes in front: *d'ól mé* → *níor ól mé*, *ar ól tú?*

**Answers still repeat the verb, in the past form.** *Ar cheannaigh tú leabhar?* is answered *Cheannaigh* or *Níor cheannaigh*. *Ar thaitin sé leat?* is answered *Thaitin* or *Níor thaitin*. Notice Budi answers *Labhair!* — one word, and it's a full answer.

**Chuaigh, chonaic, rinne, bhí — the irregulars.** Eleven Irish verbs have past forms you can't guess, and this is where they stray furthest. *Téigh* becomes *chuaigh*; *feic* becomes *chonaic*; *déan* becomes *rinne*; *tar* becomes *tháinig*; *faigh* becomes *fuair*. The table is below, and those five are the ones you'll need most.

blocks.title: Why the last four rows don't change
items: The letters **l, n, r** can't be softened in Irish spelling, so *labhair*, *léigh*, and *rith* look the same in the past and as commands. Only the pronoun tells them apart: *Léigh!* ("read!") versus *Léigh mé* ("I read").
An **s** followed by a hard consonant (*sc-, sm-, sp-, st-*) isn't softened either: *scríobh mé*, *stop mé*.
Every other verb starting with a consonant is **always** softened. When in doubt, soften — you'll be right nine times out of ten.

blocks.text: The "we" form has its own ending: *d'ólamar*, *cheannaíomar*, *ghlanamar*. The separate form *d'ól muid* is also correct and heard more often in everyday speech, so you can use either.
How to say them: *bhí* = VEE, *dúirt* = DOORTCH, *chuala* = KHOO-uh-luh, *rinne* = RIH-nyuh, *fuair* = FOO-ir, *chonaic* = KHUH-nik, *thug* = HUG, *tháinig* = HAW-nig, *chuaigh* = KHOO-uh.

blocks.title: The five you really need right now
items: *Bhí mé* (I was) and *ní raibh mé* (I wasn't) — the most common of them all.
*Chuaigh mé* (I went) — and note its odd negative, *ní dheachaigh mé*.
*Chonaic mé* (I saw) — negative *ní fhaca mé*, said "nee AH-kuh" because *fh* is silent.
*Fuair mé* (I got) — negative *ní bhfuair mé*, the only one that takes urú after *ní*.
The other six you can just recognize for now; they'll stick on their own with use.

exercises.prompt: Put into the past tense ("I" form).
Make these sentences negative. Remember: *níor* brings séimhiú, and *d'* disappears.
Write the past form of these irregular verbs ("I" form).

items: I went to Conamara on Saturday.
I had dinner in a little restaurant.
